chunks: "I separate grounds only when I can name the problem it solves, and I do it carefully. The main reasons are these.
First, safety and isolation: if one side is mains-referenced or high voltage and the other is touchable, they can't share a ground, so I use an isolation barrier with creepage and clearance.

Second, ground loops: when two separate pieces of equipment are connected by a cable and each is grounded, the loop picks up noise and carries current; isolating or having a single connection fixes it.

Third, large or noisy return currents: a motor driver returning 5 amps through a shared conductor can lift the reference of a precision ADC by tens of millivolts, so I keep the power return and the sense or analog reference separate, and join them at one point.
Fourth, different reference potentials, like a battery negative versus a high-side sensing domain, or a chassis ground used for ESD and shield terminations that I connect through a defined path.
On a single board I usually don't cut the plane; I place noisy and quiet circuits in different regions so their return currents don't overlap, and connect them at one defined point.
If I do split, no signal crosses the split except at the bridge. And for true isolation, the signals cross through isolators, not wires."
